The core insight of the paper is that betting lines encode collective intelligence about game outcomes through a probabilistic lens. The normal approximation Pr(F>U|P=p) = Φ(p/13.588) provides a clean baseline for converting spreads into win probabilities. This mapping is grounded in the assumption that game margins are normally distributed around the spread, with σ = 13.588. The Line Difference (LD) metric evaluates how well the line predicts actual outcomes. The home-underdog ATS edge is treated as a dated empirical observation rather than a predictive kernel. These primitives form a dual structure: one for static probability estimation and another for dynamic validation. Failures arise when game outcomes deviate significantly from normality or when line movement is driven by non-fundamental factors like betting volume or public sentiment. The model assumes independence between games, which may fail during correlated events such as injuries or weather impacts.
